← the dictation prep · Ops‑to‑Mike, 2026-08-07 · not part of the museum

The light table

The two runways · the 16 pictures an entry can reach for today

Against the bouncy ball law his rule · Ops wording

Never more than two or three points of focus. The law caps what a reader is asked to hold, not what the museum is allowed to show. Humans remember one or two things. Ten things reduces the odds they keep the one that matters. It does not mean we may not show more pictures. Ten manual pages arriving is ONE point of focus — we got more of the manual — not ten.

bucketceilingassignedrunway
THE PRECIOUS BUCKET
Genuine reveals. These are what a reader remembers.
 Two or three a week. 0 nothing assigned — no runway to compute
THE DUMP BUCKET
Everything else. Fun to look at, part of the story, part of the pile.
 No ceiling. A batch of any size is one point of focus. 0 no ceiling, so no runway. A pile size, and a batch of any size is one point of focus.
UNASSIGNED
Nobody has said which bucket these are in.
 — 16 the honest state today

SO THE RUNWAY IS A BOUND AND NOT A NUMBER, AND THAT IS THE ONE HONEST THING THIS TABLE CAN SAY. Of the 16 pictures an entry can reach for today, 0 are assigned precious and 16 could be — so the precious runway runs from nothing at all to 6–8 weeks, and the whole of that gap is a judgement nobody has made. The bucket is yours — it sits beside verdict in the asset table, unset, and Ops will not derive it: a rule that called every machine photograph precious would make this table look answered while nothing had been answered.

THE FIGURE THIS REPLACES IS VOID: “16 pictures = 6–8 days of material (1.1–1.6 five-day weeks)”. It counted ASSETS against a ceiling on POINTS OF FOCUS, and it used the day rather than the week. Sixteen photographs released in four batches are four points of focus, not sixteen — and if the batches are dump they may not be points of focus at all. The arithmetic was sound and the unit was wrong, which is why nothing caught it: every input was a real measurement.
